title: Opposition 'Vote Theft' Protests Cloud Modi's 25-Year Milestone
excerpt: Narendra Modi marked a quarter-century in public office with a new “We will do it” rallying cry, even as Delhi police fortified the Election Commission of India against another day of opposition protests over voter-list revisions.
body:
• October 7, 2026 marks 25 years since Narendra Modi was sworn in as Gujarat Chief Minister on October 7, 2001 — a tenure that carried him from Gandhinagar to New Delhi in 2014 and three national victories since.
  • At the Viksit Bharat Sankalp Sabha in New Delhi, Modi unveiled a new rallying cry — "We will do it!" — tied to goals including a developed India by 2047, a top-three economy, and hosting the Olympics.
  • Delhi police beefed up security around the Election Commission of India in anticipation of "vote theft" protests. Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi was briefly detained Tuesday during a march demanding the election chief's resignation over large-scale voter-list revisions that the opposition says deleted 130 million names.
  • The milestone follows a bruising year of street pressure on the government — from summer youth protests that ended only after the education minister resigned — with key state elections due next year.

Narendra Modi marked 25 years in public office on Tuesday with a new slogan for his next chapter — even as opposition "vote theft" protests ensured the milestone would not pass unchallenged. Delhi police fortified the Election Commission of India ahead of another day of demonstrations over alleged voter-list manipulation, while the Prime Minister addressed the Viksit Bharat Sankalp Sabha in New Delhi.

The milestone and the new mantra

Modi was sworn in as Gujarat Chief Minister on October 7, 2001, replacing Keshubhai Patel at a turbulent moment — the state was still recovering from the Bhuj earthquake — and remained there until 2014, when he transitioned to national politics. Addressing the gathering on Wednesday, he said the continued trust of citizens was his greatest strength.

"Viksit Bharat by 2047 — we will do it! Say it with me! Top three economy — we will do it! Atmanirbhar Bharat — we will do it! Hosting the Olympics — we will do it!"

— Narendra Modi, at the Viksit Bharat Sankalp Sabha, New Delhi

Recalling his call for collective participation in nation-building, Modi urged the crowd to repeat the slogan after each national aspiration: taking a step into space, becoming a global manufacturing hub. "When I took oath as the Chief Minister of Gujarat on October 7, 2001, I never thought that I would reach this milestone one day," he said. "I bow my head and pay my respects to the people of the country. The trust of lakhs and crores of countrymen and the hard work of lakhs of workers have always been my greatest strength."

Senior BJP leaders lauded the milestone. Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath, addressing a parallel gathering in Lucknow, said Modi had presented India as a "capable and powerful" country, citing the economy's move from the "Fragile Five" into the world's top five and a startup ecosystem that now counts more than 2.5 lakh companies against only a few thousand a decade ago.

The protests that clouded the day

The celebrations unfolded against a running opposition campaign over electoral integrity. Deutsche Welle's live coverage noted that Delhi police had beefed up security around the Election Commission of India, likely preparing for another day of "vote theft" protests. On Tuesday, Congress leader Rahul Gandhi was briefly detained by police during a protest march demanding the election chief's resignation over large-scale voter-list revisions — a campaign the opposition says wiped 130 million names from the rolls.

It is not the first time this year that street pressure has cornered the government. In July, youth protesters ended weeks of demonstrations over leaked national exam papers that forced a resit affecting 2 million students — but only after Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned, bowing to the students' primary demand. Reuters described it as the worst political crisis of Modi's third term.

Impact and analysis

That matters because of the calendar. Key state elections are due next year, and the vote-theft campaign gives the opposition a simple, repeatable line of attack on the Modi government's most sensitive flank: the legitimacy of the electoral machinery itself.

Diaspora angle

For the Indian diaspora, the milestone is familiar fare — Modi's political endurance is a constant in NRI politics. The protest side of the story travels differently: the credibility of India's electoral machinery shapes how the diaspora talks about Indian democracy abroad, and voter-list controversies now sit alongside investment summits and diaspora rallies in that conversation.

What's next

Watch whether the opposition sustains the Election Commission protests beyond the milestone week, and how the government responds as state polls approach. The immediate test is organisational: can the "vote theft" campaign stay in the headlines once the Viksit Bharat Sankalp Sabha's slogans fade, or does it retreat to the background until the next election cycle.
